```{r setup, include = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
# the code of the benchmark is in the script code/operations_benchmark.R, from
# which the chunks below are read (purl = FALSE because pkgdown purls this
# file from the package root when looking for images, where this relative
# path does not exist)
knitr::read_chunk("code/operations_benchmark.R")
# the results of the benchmark, saved by the script
benchmark <- readRDS("benchmark-results.rds")
```

`tidytracks` works on `move2` objects, and many of its functions do what
other packages for tracking data also do. This article compares how long
`tidytracks` takes for three common operations with other packages that
offer them:

- the distance between consecutive locations of each track (step lengths),
  with `move2` (Kranstauber et al. 2024), `amt` (Signer et al. 2019) and
  `trip` (Sumner 2011);
- the speed filter of McConnell et al. (1992), with `trip`, from which
  `tidytracks` ported it;
- splitting the tracks of a central place forager into trips away from its
  nest, with `track2KBA` (Beal et al. 2021).

It also shows how the time of each operation grows with the length of the
tracks and with their number, which separates the cost of each location from
the overhead of each track.

The benchmark takes about `r round(benchmark$run_minutes / 5) * 5` minutes to run, so it was run once with the
script `vignettes/articles/code/operations_benchmark.R` (in the source code
of the package), and its results are read here from
`vignettes/articles/benchmark-results.rds`. The code shown below is taken
from that script. To run it again (e.g. after changing `tidytracks`, or on
another machine), install `tidytracks` (with `R CMD INSTALL`, rather than
loading it with `devtools::load_all()`, which compiles its C++ code without
optimisation) and the other packages, and run, on an otherwise idle machine:

```sh
cd vignettes/articles
Rscript code/operations_benchmark.R
```

which overwrites `benchmark-results.rds`; then render this article again.
`Rscript code/operations_benchmark.R quick` runs everything on a few small
data sets in less than a minute, to check the script, and saves its results
in a temporary directory instead. Timings depend on the machine (see
[Machine and software](#machine-and-software)), but the differences between
the packages, and how the times grow with the size of the data, should be
similar on other machines.

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
```

```{r results_packages, message = FALSE}
# to summarise and plot the results
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Simulated tracks

The tracks are those of a central place forager, such as a seabird breeding
in a colony, with a GPS location every 5 minutes. They are simulated, so that
data sets of any size can be made with the same properties:

```{r simulate-tracks}
```

For example, the first two days of three tracks (the black points are the
nests, and the lines that leave the map go to outliers):

```{r example_tracks, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3}
example_tracks <- simulate_tracks(n_tracks = 3, n_locations = 576, seed = 1)
ggplot(example_tracks, aes(lon, lat)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(
    aes(nest_lon, nest_lat),
    data = distinct(example_tracks, id, nest_lon, nest_lat),
    colour = "black",
    size = 2
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~id) +
  coord_quickmap(
    xlim = mean(example_tracks$nest_lon) + c(-1.4, 1.4),
    ylim = mean(example_tracks$nest_lat) + c(-0.8, 0.8)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

# The data sets

The time taken by an operation on a set of tracks has two parts: one that
grows with the number of locations, and an overhead for each track (e.g.
to select its locations, or to build its results). To separate them, the
benchmark uses two series of data sets: tracks of increasing length (with
the same number of tracks), and the same total number of locations split
into an increasing number of tracks (from a few long tracks to many short
ones):

```{r data-sets, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r data-sets-table, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r table_data_sets, echo = FALSE}
data_sets <- benchmark$timings %>%
  distinct(tracks, locations) %>%
  # the series of longer tracks first, then the other data sets
  arrange(tracks != benchmark$series$tracks, tracks, locations) %>%
  mutate(
    total = tracks * locations,
    days = locations * 5 / (60 * 24),
    series = case_when(
      tracks == benchmark$series$tracks & total == benchmark$series$total ~
        "both",
      tracks == benchmark$series$tracks ~ "longer tracks",
      TRUE ~ "more tracks"
    )
  )
data_sets %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      c(tracks, locations, total),
      ~ formatC(.x, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
    ),
    days = formatC(signif(days, 2), format = "fg", digits = 2)
  ) %>%
  select(tracks, locations, days, total, series) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Tracks", "Locations per track", "Days per track", "Total locations",
      "Series"
    ),
    align = "rrrrl"
  )
```

# Running the operations

Each package works on its own class of objects: a `move2` object for
`tidytracks` and `move2`, a `track_xyt` for `amt`, a `trip` object (a
`SpatialPointsDataFrame` from `sp`) for `trip`, and data frames for
`track2KBA`. These are built from the data frame of locations of each data
set (outside of the timings):

```{r inputs, eval = FALSE}
```

The operations are then run with each package, on all the tracks of a data
set:

```{r operations, eval = FALSE}
```

The settings are matched so that the packages give the same results:

- **Step distances**: `tidytracks` and `trip` compute geodesic distances on
  the WGS84 ellipsoid (with the `geodist` package), whereas `move2` and `amt`
  use `sf::st_distance()`, which, with `s2` (the default of `sf`), computes
  great circle distances on a sphere. `tidytracks`, `move2` and `amt` give
  `NA` for the last location of each track, and `trip` gives 0. `amt` measures
  the steps of a single track, so its tracks are nested and measured in
  turn, as in its documentation, and this is included in its time.
- **Speed filter**: `tidytracks` and `trip` run the same algorithm, with a
  maximum speed of 120 km/h (`trip` takes it in km/h, for longitudes and
  latitudes). The optional check of the first and last locations of each
  track of `tidytracks` is off by default.
- **Trips**: both packages use the nest of each animal, start a trip when
  the animal goes further than 5 km from it, end it when it comes back
  within 5 km, and keep the locations at the nest. `track2KBA` drops trips
  shorter than a minimum duration, which is set to 0 here, as `tidytracks`
  has none.

Each operation is run once, as a warm-up, which also gives the results
compared below, and then, if that took less than a minute, again until
these runs have taken a minute (but at least three and at most ten times),
of which the median time is reported:

```{r timing, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r run-benchmark, eval = FALSE}
```

# Do the packages give the same results?

The results of each package are compared with those of `tidytracks`, on each
data set:

```{r checks, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r check_numbers, include = FALSE}
checks <- benchmark$checks
# the value of a check, summed over all the data sets
check_total <- function(operation, package, check) {
  sum(checks$value[
    checks$operation == operation & checks$package == package &
      checks$check == check
  ])
}
# the largest relative difference between step distances, over all the data
# sets
distance_diff <- function(package) {
  max(checks$value[
    checks$operation == "distance" & checks$package == package
  ])
}
# in %, for move2 and amt
s2_diff <- signif(100 * max(distance_diff("move2"), distance_diff("amt")), 2)
# the text below assumes that the distances of trip and tidytracks are the
# same (up to rounding errors)
stopifnot(distance_diff("trip") < 1e-9)
# the checks of the speed filter, with one row per data set, and whether
# tidytracks flags exactly the simulated outliers
speed_checks <- checks %>%
  filter(operation == "speed_filter") %>%
  mutate(
    check = recode(
      check,
      "outliers among the first two or last two locations of a track" =
        "end_outliers",
      "locations flagged" = "flagged",
      "outliers flagged" = "outliers_flagged",
      "locations flagged differently" = "differ",
      "tracks with locations flagged differently" = "tracks_differ",
      "tracks with an outlier second to last, flagged differently" =
        "tracks_differ_end"
    )
  ) %>%
  select(tracks, locations, check, value) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = check, values_from = value) %>%
  mutate(exact = flagged == outliers & outliers_flagged == outliers)
# the data set on which it does not (the text below assumes that there is
# one, and that all the tracks in which tidytracks and trip flag different
# locations have an outlier as their second-to-last location)
inexact <- filter(speed_checks, !exact)
stopifnot(
  nrow(inexact) == 1,
  sum(speed_checks$tracks_differ) == sum(speed_checks$tracks_differ_end)
)
# the text below also assumes that tidytracks and track2KBA put the same
# locations in trips, except at the ends of trips and tracks
stopifnot(
  check_total(
    "trip_split", "both", "other locations in a trip in only one package"
  ) == 0
)
```

- **Step distances**: the distances of `trip` are the same as those of
  `tidytracks` (up to rounding errors), and those of `move2` and `amt` differ from them by at most `r s2_diff`%,
  as they are measured on a sphere rather than on the ellipsoid.
- **Speed filter**: the filter of McConnell et al. (1992) computes, for each
  location, the root mean square of four speeds (from the previous location
  and to the next one, and from and to the locations two steps away). In each
  run of locations where this exceeds the maximum speed, it flags the
  location where it is largest, and it then does it again on the locations
  not flagged, until none exceeds the maximum speed. It cannot flag the first
  two and last two locations of a track (their root mean square speed is set
  to 0). `tidytracks` flags exactly the simulated outliers in
  `r sum(speed_checks$exact)` of the `r nrow(speed_checks)` data sets. In the
  data set of `r format(inexact$tracks, big.mark = ",")` tracks of
  `r format(inexact$locations, big.mark = ",")` locations,
  `r inexact$end_outliers` of the `r inexact$outliers` outliers are among the
  first two or last two locations of a track: they are not flagged, and
  `r inexact$flagged - inexact$outliers_flagged` other locations of the same
  tracks are flagged instead (`tidytracks` has an option, `check_first_last`,
  to also check the first and last locations of each track, which is off by
  default). `tidytracks` and `trip` flag the same locations, except
  `r sum(speed_checks$differ)` locations in
  `r sum(speed_checks$tracks_differ)` tracks, whose second-to-last location
  is an outlier: `tidytracks` then flags the locations
  before the outlier, one at a time, until the speeds to the outlier are
  low enough, whereas `trip` flags only the location just before it. This is
  because `trip` (in version
  `r benchmark$session$value[benchmark$session$item == "trip"]`) computes the
  speeds between locations two steps apart wrongly for longitudes and
  latitudes: given four vectors of coordinates, `trip::trackDistance()`
  returns the distances between consecutive points, rather than between the
  pairs of points given.
- **Trips**: `tidytracks` and `track2KBA` find the same trips, with the same
  locations, except at the ends of trips and of tracks. `track2KBA` includes
  in each trip the first location back within 5 km of the nest
  (`r format(check_total("trip_split", "track2KBA", "returns to the nest in a trip"), big.mark = ",")`
  locations in all), and, when the last location of a track is the first
  one beyond 5 km of the nest, `tidytracks` makes it a trip of its own (an
  incomplete one), whereas `track2KBA` does not
  (`r check_total("trip_split", "tidytracks", "trips of the last location of a track")`
  trips). `tidytracks` thus finds
  `r format(check_total("trip_split", "tidytracks", "trips"), big.mark = ",")`
  trips, and `track2KBA`
  `r format(check_total("trip_split", "track2KBA", "trips"), big.mark = ",")`.
  No other location is in a trip in only one of them.

# How long do they take?

```{r read_timings}
operation_labels <- c(
  distance = "Step distances",
  speed_filter = "Speed filter",
  trip_split = "Trips"
)
package_levels <- c("tidytracks", "move2", "amt", "trip", "track2KBA")
timings <- benchmark$timings %>%
  mutate(
    total = tracks * locations,
    operation = factor(operation_labels[operation], operation_labels),
    package = factor(package, package_levels)
  )
# the two series: tracks of increasing length, and the same total number of
# locations in more and more tracks
series_tracks <- benchmark$series$tracks
series_total <- benchmark$series$total
longer_tracks <- timings %>%
  filter(tracks == series_tracks)
more_tracks <- timings %>%
  filter(total == series_total)
```

```{r timing_numbers, include = FALSE}
# the time (s) of an operation with a package, on a data set
time_of <- function(operation, package, tracks, locations) {
  timings$seconds[
    timings$operation == operation_labels[[operation]] &
      timings$package == package &
      timings$tracks == tracks &
      timings$locations == locations
  ]
}
# a number with 2 significant digits, for the text
fmt <- function(x) {
  formatC(signif(x, 2), format = "fg", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
}
# the time on a data set, and relative to tidytracks
secs <- function(operation, package, tracks, locations) {
  fmt(time_of(operation, package, tracks, locations))
}
ratio <- function(operation, package, tracks, locations) {
  fmt(
    time_of(operation, package, tracks, locations) /
      time_of(operation, "tidytracks", tracks, locations)
  )
}
# the data sets of each series
track_lengths <- sort(unique(longer_tracks$locations))
longest <- max(track_lengths)
track_counts <- sort(unique(more_tracks$tracks))
most <- max(track_counts)
# the largest data set (the longest tracks), and the data set with the most
# tracks
largest <- c(series_tracks, longest)
many <- c(most, series_total / most)
single <- c(1, series_total)
# the time per location (in microseconds) on the largest data set
per_location <- function(operation, package) {
  fmt(
    1e6 * time_of(operation, package, largest[1], largest[2]) /
      prod(largest)
  )
}
# how many times longer an operation takes on tracks 10 times as long, in the
# series of longer tracks
growth <- function(operation, package, locations) {
  fmt(
    time_of(operation, package, series_tracks, 10 * locations) /
      time_of(operation, package, series_tracks, locations)
  )
}
# the overhead of each track (in ms), from the times on the same locations in
# the most tracks and in the series_tracks tracks (rather than in a single
# track, on which the speed filter and track2KBA take longer)
per_track <- function(operation, package) {
  many_time <- time_of(operation, package, many[1], many[2])
  few_time <- time_of(
    operation, package, series_tracks, series_total / series_tracks
  )
  fmt(1000 * (many_time - few_time) / (most - series_tracks))
}
# the time that track2KBA would take on the largest data set (in minutes),
# from its time on a single track of the same length
kba_largest <- round(
  series_tracks * time_of("trip_split", "track2KBA", 1, longest) / 60
)
```

The times of the operations on the two series of data sets are shown below
(on log scales), and in the table at the end of this section.

```{r plot_functions}
# one colour per package
package_colours <- c(
  tidytracks = "#2a78d6",
  move2 = "#8e5bd0",
  amt = "#eb6834",
  trip = "#1baf7a",
  track2KBA = "#c4373b"
)
# the times of a series of data sets, with one panel per operation
series_plot <- function(data, x, x_label) {
  # nolint next: object_usage_linter.
  ggplot(data, aes(x = {{ x }}, y = seconds, colour = package)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    facet_wrap(~operation, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
    scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number(drop0trailing = TRUE)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = package_colours) +
    labs(x = x_label, y = "Time (s, log scale)", colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.spacing.x = unit(1.5, "lines"),
      # room for the last label of the x axis
      plot.margin = margin(5.5, 15, 5.5, 5.5),
      legend.position = "top"
    )
}
```

## Longer tracks

```{r plot_longer_tracks, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.4}
series_plot(
  longer_tracks,
  locations,
  paste0(
    "Locations per track (", series_tracks, " tracks, log scale)"
  )
)
```

With `r series_tracks` tracks, the time of the operations grows about in
proportion to the number of locations (a bit less from the smallest data
set, on which fixed costs, such as checking the inputs, take a larger share
of the time), except for `track2KBA`, whose time grows faster:

- **Step distances**: `tidytracks` is the fastest, with
  `r secs("distance", "tidytracks", largest[1], largest[2])` s for the
  `r fmt(prod(largest))` locations of the largest data set (about
  `r per_location("distance", "tidytracks")` µs per location): `move2` takes
  `r ratio("distance", "move2", largest[1], largest[2])` times as long, `amt`
  `r ratio("distance", "amt", largest[1], largest[2])` times and `trip`
  `r ratio("distance", "trip", largest[1], largest[2])` times.
- **Speed filter**: `tidytracks` and `trip` run the same algorithm, in R,
  and take similar times: `r secs("speed_filter", "tidytracks", largest[1], largest[2])` s
  and `r secs("speed_filter", "trip", largest[1], largest[2])` s on the
  largest data set. The filter computes the speeds of the whole track again
  after removing each batch of outliers, so it takes longer than the step
  distances (about `r per_location("speed_filter", "tidytracks")` µs per
  location with `tidytracks`).
- **Trips**: `tidytracks` splits the largest data set into trips in
  `r secs("trip_split", "tidytracks", largest[1], largest[2])` s (about
  `r per_location("trip_split", "tidytracks")` µs per location). `track2KBA`
  is much slower: it takes
  `r ratio("trip_split", "track2KBA", series_tracks, track_lengths[2])`
  times as long as `tidytracks` on `r series_tracks` tracks of
  `r fmt(track_lengths[2])` locations. Its time also grows faster than the
  length of the tracks, as it goes through the locations of each track one
  at a time, in R, and updates the whole track at many of these steps: with
  tracks ten times as long (from `r fmt(track_lengths[1])` to
  `r fmt(track_lengths[2])` locations), it takes
  `r growth("trip_split", "track2KBA", track_lengths[1])` times as long, and
  it takes `r secs("trip_split", "track2KBA", 1, longest)` s on a single
  track of `r fmt(longest)` locations (see below). It was thus not run on the
  largest data set, on which it would take more than `r kba_largest`
  minutes.

## More tracks

```{r plot_more_tracks, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.4}
series_plot(
  more_tracks,
  tracks,
  paste0(
    "Number of tracks (", fmt(series_total), " locations in all, log scale)"
  )
)
```

With the same `r fmt(series_total)` locations in more and more tracks, the
time of the operations that handle each track in turn grows with the number
of tracks:

- **Step distances**: `tidytracks` and `move2` compute the distances of all
  the tracks at once, so their time hardly depends on the number of tracks
  (`r secs("distance", "tidytracks", many[1], many[2])` s with `tidytracks`
  for `r fmt(most)` tracks, against
  `r secs("distance", "tidytracks", single[1], single[2])` s for a single
  track). `amt` and `trip` measure each track in turn, which adds about
  `r per_track("distance", "amt")` ms and `r per_track("distance", "trip")` ms
  per track respectively: with `r fmt(most)` tracks of `r fmt(many[2])`
  locations, `amt` takes `r ratio("distance", "amt", many[1], many[2])` times as
  long as `tidytracks`, and `trip` `r ratio("distance", "trip", many[1], many[2])`
  times.
- **Speed filter**: both packages filter each track in turn, which adds
  about `r per_track("speed_filter", "tidytracks")` ms per track with
  `tidytracks`, and `r per_track("speed_filter", "trip")` ms with `trip`.
  A single track of `r fmt(series_total)` locations takes longer than
  `r series_tracks` tracks of `r fmt(series_total / series_tracks)`, though:
  the filter goes over a whole track again until no location exceeds the
  maximum speed, and a long track tends to need more passes.
- **Trips**: both packages split each track in turn. `tidytracks` adds about
  `r per_track("trip_split", "tidytracks")` ms per track (to find the
  locations of the track, and build the metadata of its trips), so that
  `r fmt(most)` tracks of `r fmt(many[2])` locations take
  `r secs("trip_split", "tidytracks", many[1], many[2])` s, against
  `r secs("trip_split", "tidytracks", single[1], single[2])` s for a single
  track of `r fmt(series_total)` locations. `track2KBA` is slowest both on
  a single long track (as its time grows faster than the length of the
  tracks) and on many short tracks: it takes
  `r secs("trip_split", "track2KBA", many[1], many[2])` s on the
  `r fmt(most)` tracks, `r ratio("trip_split", "track2KBA", many[1], many[2])`
  times as long as `tidytracks`, as it adds the trips of each track to those
  of the previous tracks with `rbind()`, which copies them all each time, so
  that this part of its time grows with the square of the number of
  tracks.

```{r table_timings, echo = FALSE}
# one column per package; empty for the packages that do not have an
# operation, and "not run" for track2KBA on the largest data set
timings %>%
  complete(nesting(operation, package), nesting(tracks, locations)) %>%
  mutate(
    seconds = ifelse(
      is.na(seconds),
      "not run",
      formatC(signif(seconds, 2), format = "fg", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
    ),
    data_set = paste(
      formatC(tracks, format = "d", big.mark = ","), "x",
      formatC(locations, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
    )
  ) %>%
  # the series of longer tracks first, then the other data sets
  arrange(tracks != series_tracks, tracks, locations, operation, package) %>%
  mutate(data_set = factor(data_set, unique(data_set))) %>%
  select(data_set, operation, package, seconds) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = package, values_from = seconds, values_fill = "") %>%
  select(data_set, operation, any_of(package_levels)) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Tracks x locations per track", "Operation",
      intersect(package_levels, levels(timings$package))
    ),
    align = "llrrrrr",
    caption = paste(
      "Time (s) of each operation on all the tracks of each data set",
      "(median of up to ten runs, or a single run for the runs of more than",
      "a minute)."
    )
  )
```

# Summary

```{r summary_numbers, include = FALSE}
# the range of the times of the other packages relative to tidytracks, for
# the step distances on the largest data set
distance_ratios <- vapply(
  c("move2", "amt", "trip"),
  function(package) {
    time_of("distance", package, largest[1], largest[2]) /
      time_of("distance", "tidytracks", largest[1], largest[2])
  },
  numeric(1)
)
distance_ratios <- fmt(range(distance_ratios))
```

- Given the same settings, the packages give the same results, except at
  the ends of some tracks and trips (see above), and up to the differences
  between geodesic distances and distances on a sphere.
- `tidytracks` is the fastest for the three operations. On
  `r series_tracks` tracks of `r fmt(longest)` locations, it computes the
  step distances in `r secs("distance", "tidytracks", largest[1], largest[2])` s,
  whereas the other packages take `r distance_ratios[1]` to
  `r distance_ratios[2]` times as long, and it splits the tracks into trips
  in `r secs("trip_split", "tidytracks", largest[1], largest[2])` s, whereas
  `track2KBA`, whose time grows faster than the length and the number of the
  tracks, would take more than `r kba_largest` minutes. Its speed filter,
  which runs the same algorithm as that of `trip`, takes
  `r secs("speed_filter", "tidytracks", largest[1], largest[2])` s, and
  `trip` `r ratio("speed_filter", "trip", largest[1], largest[2])` times as
  long.
- The operations that handle each track in turn have an overhead for each
  track, of up to a few milliseconds, which matters only for data sets with
  many short tracks. `tidytracks` (and `move2`) compute the step distances
  of all the tracks at once, without such an overhead.
